title: Patellofemoral Pain Diagnosis | PFPS Diagnosis & Assessment
purpose: Overview of diagnosing patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS): anterior knee pain during running, squatting or stairs; affects all ages and persists for years in up to 60% of cases.
structure: Patellofemoral joint: altered loading on a flexed knee; hypotheses include abnormal patellofemoral alignment/trochlear morphology (poor patellar tracking) and weakness of quadriceps and glutes (femoral internal rotation altering the leg axis).
procedure: Diagnosis of exclusion after other pathologies are ruled out. Proposed diagnostic clusters all have weak clinical value; the single best available finding is anterior knee pain while squatting.
positive: Anterior knee pain while squatting: PFPS is evident in 80% of people with this finding.

accuracy.source: n/a (page cites Crossley et al. 2016 consensus statement)

notes: Related tests: decline step-down test, Clarke's sign, patellofemoral pain cluster.

title: Patellofemoral Pain Cluster | PFPS Diagnosis and Assessment
purpose: Three diagnostic clusters for patellofemoral pain syndrome from Cook et al. 2010.
structure: Patellofemoral joint; functional and situational findings (muscle contraction, squatting, kneeling, peripatellar palpation).
procedure: Cluster 1: pain during muscle contraction + pain during squatting (2 of 2). Cluster 2: pain during muscle contraction and/or squatting and/or peripatellar palpation (2 of 3). Cluster 3: pain during muscle contraction + squatting + kneeling (3 of 3).
notes: All three rated weak clinical value because of modest ratios and large confidence intervals. Page has three videos (one per cluster). Related tests: decline step-down, Clarke's sign.

title: Clarke's Sign | Patellar Grind Test | Patellofemoral Pain Assessment
purpose: Identify pathological changes of the retropatellar cartilage by compressing the patella during quadriceps contraction.
procedure: Patient supine with knees extended. Examiner on the involved side places the web space of the thumb on the superior border of the patella and applies downward and inferior pressure while the patient contracts the quadriceps as if extending the knee.
positive: Pain with patellar movement or inability to complete the test.

accuracy.source: Cook et al. 2012 systematic review (no high-quality studies); also cited Nijs et al. 2006

notes: Weak clinical value. Related tests: patellar apprehension, moving patellar apprehension, decline step-down.

title: Decline Step Down Test | Patellofemoral Pain
purpose: Performance test for patellofemoral pain measuring the maximal pain-free knee flexion angle while stepping down on a decline, since descending stairs is a hallmark symptom.
structure: Patellofemoral joint under eccentric quadriceps load.
procedure: SOURCE ISSUE: the page's execution paragraph is copied from the Clarke's sign page (supine patellar compression with quadriceps contraction) and does not describe the decline step-down; the actual execution (step-down from a decline board, recording the maximal pain-free flexion angle) is only in the video and in Ophey et al. 2019.
positive: Outcome is the maximal pain-free flexion angle (per the page's description of Ophey et al. 2019); the page's 'positive' sentence is copied from Clarke's sign.

accuracy.source: Reliability/validity only: Ophey et al. 2019, 'perfect' intra- and inter-observer reliability, average but significant construct validity vs the anterior knee pain scale

notes: Page rates moderate clinical value as a performance/outcome test. Related tests: patellar apprehension, moving patellar apprehension, Clarke's sign.
status: ok (source text duplicates Clarke's sign procedure)

title: Patellar Apprehension Test | Patella Dislocation Assessment
purpose: Assess lateral patellar instability / history of patellar dislocation.
structure: Patella and medial soft-tissue restraints; risk factors include sulcus angle and depth, genetic predisposition.
procedure: Patient supine, knee 30° flexion, quadriceps relaxed. With both thumbs on the medial side of the patella, push it laterally to maximal displacement.
positive: Apprehension or discomfort at maximal lateral displacement; the patient may grab the examiner's hands or straighten the knee to pull the patella back.

accuracy.source: Nunes et al. 2013 systematic review/meta-analysis (clinical tests for PFPS); also cited Malanga et al. 2003

notes: Weak clinical value. Alternative: moving patellar apprehension test.

title: Moving Patellar Apprehension Test | Patella Dislocation
purpose: Dynamic test (Ahmad et al. 2009) that mimics a patellar dislocation/instability episode, for cases the static apprehension test, CT or MRI may miss.
structure: Patella engaging the trochlea during flexion; medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) and medial soft tissues guide the patella into the trochlea; the patella subluxates most easily at about 20° flexion.
procedure: Patient supine with the lower leg over the edge of the bench. Part 1: in full extension the examiner translates the patella laterally with a thumb, flexes the knee to 90° watching for verbal apprehension or quadriceps contraction to stop flexion/reposition the patella, then returns to extension keeping the lateral translation. Part 2: in full extension translate the patella medially as far as possible with the index finger and flex to 90°; apprehension and quadriceps contraction should disappear.
positive: Both parts positive: apprehension with lateral translation in part 1 and elimination of apprehension with medial translation in part 2.

accuracy.source: Ahmad et al. 2009 diagnostic cohort, overall accuracy 94.1% (excluded symptomatic subluxations; not validated by other studies)

notes: Page rates moderate clinical value. Concept similar to the pivot shift (ACL), release test (shoulder) and moving valgus stress test (elbow). Alternative: patellar apprehension test.

title: Hoffa's Test | Infrapatellar Fat Pad Syndrome Assessment
purpose: Detect impingement of the infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad as an often-overlooked source of anterior knee pain.
structure: Infrapatellar fat pad: intracapsular, extrasynovial, highly vascularized and innervated, from the inferior patellar pole to the proximal tibia.
procedure: Patient supine, knee 30-60° flexion. One hand supports the tibia from behind while the other presses directly on the medial and lateral sides of the inferior patellar pole. Repeat with the knee extended.
positive: More pain on pressure (either side) in extension than in flexion.

accuracy.source: n/a: not evaluated in diagnostic studies (Dragoo et al. 2012)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Must be distinguished from patellofemoral pain (see PFPS diagnosis, PFPS cluster, decline step-down, Clarke's sign).

title: Patellar Tendon Palpation | Patellar Tendinopathy Assessment
purpose: Palpation for patellar tendinopathy, a frequent anterior knee pain entity in jumping sports (volleyball, basketball, track and field).
structure: Patellar tendon, especially its attachment at the inferior pole of the patella.
procedure: Patient supine. Gently palpate the patellar tendon at its attachment over the inferior pole of the patella and along its whole length from proximal to distal.

accuracy.source: Cook et al. 2001 (vs ultrasound, young basketball players); Maffulli et al. 2017 (different ultrasound criteria and recruitment setting)

notes: Clinical value as a stand-alone test remains moderate given the conflicting figures. Related test: Royal London Hospital test (knee).

title: Royal London Hospital Test Knee | Patellar Tendinopathy Exam
purpose: Diagnose patellar tendinopathy by comparing tendon tenderness with the knee extended versus flexed (adapted from the Achilles version).
structure: Patellar tendon; tenderness changes when the tendon is under tension.
procedure: Patient supine. Palpate the tendon from proximal to distal with the knee extended to find local tenderness, then palpate the same portion with the knee flexed to 90° (tendon under tension).
positive: Pain markedly reduced or absent in knee flexion. The mechanism is unknown.

accuracy.source: Maffulli et al. 2017 (small sample of 30 patients)

notes: Clinical value rated moderate because the sample is small and the ultrasound criteria/recruitment differ from Cook et al. 2001 (palpation Sn 68%, Sp 9%). Related test: patellar tendon palpation.

title: Noble's Test | Noble Compression Test | ITBS / Runner's Knee Assessment
purpose: Provocation test for iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS, runner's knee), an overuse injury of endurance athletes.
structure: Distal iliotibial band over the lateral femoral epicondyle; proposed mechanisms are friction, compression of the underlying fat pad/connective tissue, or bursitis. Evidence that hip abductor weakness is causal is limited/conflicting (van der Worp et al. 2012).
procedure: Knee flexed to 90°, pressure applied on or 1-2 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle, then the knee is gradually extended.
positive: Severe pain over the lateral epicondyle at about 30° flexion, of the same quality as during running (the ITB passes over the condyle at that angle).
notes: ITBS is diagnosed from history and presentation; clinical value questionable. Related: Renne's test, ITBS rehab page.

title: Renne's Test | Iliotibial Band Syndrome / Runner's Knee Assessment
purpose: Provocation test for iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS, runner's knee).
structure: Distal iliotibial band over the lateral femoral epicondyle (same background as Noble's test).
procedure: SOURCE ISSUE: the page's execution paragraph is identical to the Noble's test page (pressure on the lateral epicondyle at 90° flexion, then extension). Renne's original weight-bearing description (Renne 1975) is not in the page text; refer to the video.
positive: Per the page text: severe pain over the lateral epicondyle at about 30° flexion, same quality as running pain (identical to Noble's page).
notes: Clinical value questionable. Related: Noble's compression test, ITBS rehab page.
status: ok (source text duplicates Noble's test procedure)
